name: Online feature store for tabular fraud/risk classifiers
category: Adjacent — generic online feature store role (fraud/risk slice)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Online feature store role for tabular fraud / risk classifiers (XGBoost / LightGBM / TabNet / TabTransformer)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: An ML platform or risk team must serve 20–100+ pre-computed per-entity features to a tabular fraud / risk classifier inside a <100 ms request budget with point-in-time parity against the training data the same features were materialised from offline.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete jobs: (1) Provide the online half of a fraud / risk feature store so an XGBoost / LightGBM / TabNet / TabTransformer scorer can hydrate its 20–100+ feature vector in a single batched lookup at decision time (Stripe Radar, Coinbase, Plaid Signal, JPMorgan Chase all serve this pattern at <10–100 ms p99). (2) Guarantee training-serving parity by emitting the same feature values online as the offline / training pipeline materialised against historical events — eliminating the 'features stale at 5 minutes' or 'offline transformation diverged from online' failure modes that Feast, Tecton, and Hopsworks all explicitly market against. (3) Act as the low-latency last-mile lookup layer in front of a classifier when the team's existing offline feature store (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, S3 + Iceberg) cannot meet the <10 ms feature-fetch budget; the buyer wants a 'Redis-class' KV with first-class aggregation primitives instead of a Lua-on-Redis ad-hoc pile.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Whatever raw events feed the classifier's features land in beava as @bv.event records — the framing in this category is deliberately classifier-shape-agnostic, but the dominant shapes are: charge_attempt / authorization, login_attempt, signup, withdrawal, ach_transfer, claim_filed, account_mutation (email/phone/password/address change), device_seen, ip_seen, kyc_check, dispute_filed, chargeback. Beyond the raw transactional events, the online FS also accepts pre-computed feature 'pushes' from upstream Spark / Flink / DBT jobs (the Feast / Tecton pattern of 'materialise offline, write to online store') — beava would receive these as direct @bv.event writes carrying already-aggregated values rather than running its own aggregation, which is the alternative integration mode for buyers whose offline pipeline is already authoritative.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: 20–100+ features per decision, expressed across the standard set of online-FS feature shapes: (a) entity-level counters and sums (count(charges, 24h), sum(amount, 7d) per card_hash / account_id / device_id / ip), (b) velocities and rates (txn_per_min, decline_rate_1h), (c) n_unique sketches over high-cardinality fan-outs (n_unique(merchant_id, 24h) per card, n_unique(card_hash, 1h) per device — typically HLL-backed), (d) distances and impossible-travel signals (max-geo-distance(login_ip_geo, 1h)), (e) distributions over amount / decline_code / mcc (CMS top-K, t-digest percentiles), (f) time-since-last-X (seconds since last decline, days since last password change), (g) ratio / divergence features (current_amount / avg_amount_30d), (h) on-demand / request-time features that are deterministic functions of the request payload itself (Tecton 'on-demand feature views') and that beava would have to support via the SDK rather than as state. The beava primitive set (50+ aggregation operators per the README) covers (a)–(f) natively; (g) is a derived shape and (h) is an integration shape.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Multiple parallel grains — the defining characteristic of an online FS for fraud is that a single decision composes features from 4–8 different primary keys: card_hash, account_id / user_id, device_id (fingerprint), ip, bin, email_hash, ship_address_hash, merchant_id, (card_hash × merchant_id) pair, (account_id × counterparty) pair, wallet_address, IMEI / IMSI (mobile fraud), API key (B2B abuse). Beava's per-@bv.table per-key model maps directly; the open question is whether the buyer needs cross-grain joins or just parallel batch_get fan-out (the latter is the common case).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate (1m, 5m, 10m, 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d) because velocity rules and rate features need rolling counts. Tumbling windows show up for accounting-grade fraud-rate reporting. Session windows show up for ATO and behavioural-sequence features (Coinbase's user-sequence framework). Both exact (counters, sums, time-since-last) and approximate (HLL n_unique, CMS top-K, t-digest percentiles) aggregates are first-class — exact for regulatory and billing-grade features, approximate for high-cardinality device / IP fan-outs where 1–2 % error is invisible compared to model variance. Point-in-time correctness on the offline side (the training data must reflect feature values 'as of' the event timestamp, not 'as of now') is a hard requirement that the online store must remain consistent with — Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks all market this aggressively.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once with idempotent counters (key = event_id) is acceptable for the scorer's feature inputs because model variance dwarfs single-count duplicate error; strict exactly-once is required only when the same beava counters double as regulator-facing accounting (PSD2 TRA, chargeback liability) or as billing inputs — in which case the buyer typically separates the 'feature' and 'accounting' aggregations into different @bv.table definitions.

technical_fit.latency_budget: End-to-end request budget is typically 50–100 ms for fraud / risk scoring (Stripe Radar ~100 ms total; JPMorgan Chase reports 9 ms p99 for real-time fraud screening on Inferentia3; Coinbase 'within milliseconds' for withdrawal scoring; Tecton claims sub-10 ms feature retrieval and 0.8 ms in published references; Databricks Feature Serving claims sub-second; Vertex AI Feature Store reports ~30 ms server-side at 100 qps when Bigtable is not overloaded). Of this, the feature-fetch step itself must finish in 1–10 ms p99 to leave room for the model and the rest of the request. Beava's published sub-millisecond TCP get_many is comfortably inside this budget and is materially faster than Vertex AI Feature Store's reported ~30 ms.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Seconds to tens of seconds. Tecton explicitly markets 'sub-100 ms freshness' as a wedge; the 'features stale at 5 minutes' failure mode is the canonical motivator for moving from batch to streaming feature stores. Beava's push-on-event model produces single-digit-ms feature staleness, which exceeds every published competitor's freshness SLA.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a typical online-FS buyer in fraud / risk is 1k–50k decisions/sec (mid-market PSP, mid-bank, large fintech); large players run far higher (PayPal cited 1M TPS on Aerospike; JPMorgan Chase $2.4T daily transaction volume; a published digital-commerce rig cites ~180k writes/sec + ~75k reads/sec on a 25B-record dataset). Each decision is 1 batched read of 20–100 features plus typically 3–6 writes (one per entity grain ticked). Beava's published 684k EPS sustained on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack+parallel=16) covers single-tenant requirements for almost every buyer in this category short of the global card networks. [uncertain] exact production EPS for Tecton / Chalk / Fennel / Featureform reference customers.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Balanced to slightly read-heavy at decision time. Each transaction emits ~3–6 entity-grain writes and 1 batched read of 20–100 features, but the batched read costs more per call than a single write because it fans out across multiple keys; net effect is roughly balanced. Pure ranking / scoring workloads with no event ingestion would be read-heavy, but fraud / risk uses the same store for both materialisation and serving.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order-of-magnitude per buyer in this category: mid-market fintech with ~10M active entities × ~5 grains × ~30–50 features × ~16 bytes/counter ≈ 24–40 GB hot state — well inside a single beava box. A large bank or global PSP with ~1B entities pushes into hundreds of GB to low TB, which exceeds today's single-binary in-memory ceiling and forces buyer-side sharding (partition by tenant / region / BIN range across multiple beava processes) or a wait for in-process sharding. Note: SageMaker Online Feature Store and Tecton both rely on DynamoDB / Redis for the online tier specifically because state can grow beyond a single-machine memory budget; this is beava's headline gap in this category at the very top of the market.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Explosive on ip and device_id (proxy pools, botnets), slowly-growing on account_id and bin, bounded on merchant_id and on the rules engine's feature names. Buyers in this category routinely run into 100M–10B unique entities across all grains combined when integrated with the offline tier; HLL / CMS sketches are the standard mitigation and are part of beava's 50+ primitive set.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed. Hot velocity counters: seconds to days (1m / 10m / 1h / 24h / 7d). Per-entity behavioural profile state: 30–90 days. Regulator-mandated retention (chargebacks, AML, KYC linkage): 540 days to multiple years (lives in the offline store, not the online hot tier). Beava's WAL+snapshot+in-memory posture fits the seconds-to-days hot tier cleanly; the multi-year tail is the offline FS's job and is not where beava plays.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–100+ per decision. Stripe explicitly motivates 'hundreds of features' in Radar; real-world XGBoost / LightGBM fraud models commonly use 30–100 engineered features; Coinbase's sequence-feature framework adds 10s more. Beava's batch_get is the right shape for this fan-out and is one of the strongest fits in this category.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is the floor — recent counters must survive a process restart or velocity rules are blind during the recovery window. Regulator-grade durability is NOT required of the online FS itself in this category; that lives in the offline store / system of record. Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot + refuse-on-network-FS matches the crash-safe tier required of an online FS; competitors achieve the same with Redis AOF, DynamoDB write-ahead logging, or Cassandra commit logs, all of which beava is functionally equivalent to for this tier. Where beava is meaningfully different is the refuse-on-network-FS stance, which buyers running on EFS / EBS-only fleets will need to plan around.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional or single-binary per-tenant fits a mid-market fintech or a single-team ML platform. Multi-region active-active is the gap: every managed competitor (Tecton, SageMaker Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store, Databricks Feature Serving) ships cross-region replication out of the box for buyers running global authorization paths; beava does not in v0. A 'feature platform vendor hosting multiple tenants on one box' deployment is also blocked by lack of multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs.

commercial_fit.who_buys: ML platform team is the primary buyer in this framing (the team that owns the online feature store as infrastructure), with the risk / fraud team as the consuming customer. Secondary buyers include the data engineering / streaming team (if they own the materialisation pipeline) and the platform-engineering / SRE team (if they own the KV / cache tier the online FS sits on). Tecton, Feast, Hopsworks, Chalk, and Fennel all sell to the ML platform team as primary buyer.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Two overlapping markets are relevant: (a) the broader MLOps market — projected $4.39 B in 2026 growing to $89.91 B by 2034 at ~45.8% CAGR (Fortune Business Insights) or $2.19 B in 2024 to $16.6 B by 2030 at ~40.5% CAGR (Grand View) — within which feature stores are a fast-growing line item; (b) the fraud detection & prevention market — $52.06 B in 2026 to $146.25 B by 2033 at ~15.9% CAGR (Coherent Market Insights). Within those, BFSI is the leading vertical (~25.9% share) and fraud / risk is the highest-paid online-FS use case. Tecton (acquired by Databricks 2025) is the most visible specialist vendor; Hopsworks, Chalk, Fennel, Featureform, Tacnode are well-funded; Feast is the open-source default and is hosted by the Linux Foundation. [uncertain] feature-store sub-segment revenue is not separately broken out in the public market reports.
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Three forces: (1) Training-serving skew — the canonical online-FS pain point that buyers fail to fix with 'just use Redis' rigs and that drives them toward a real feature store; recent dev.to commentary ('Why Feature Stores Didn't Fix Training–Serving Skew') shows this is still an active problem in 2025. (2) Fraud loss curve — CNP fraud losses growing double-digit % / year, ATO and ACH fraud both rising; risk teams escalate to ML platform for 'real-time features now'. (3) Cost and consolidation — buyers are looking at their (Kafka + Flink + Redis + offline FS) bill and asking whether a single-binary 'Redis with primitives' can collapse the stack; the Databricks acquisition of Tecton in 2025 signals consolidation pressure.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Buyer-side constraints flow from the consuming domain (PSD2 / PSD3 SCA + TRA for EU payments, PCI-DSS v4.0.1 for card data, FFIEC and OCC for US banking, GLBA, BSA / FinCEN for AML, GDPR / CCPA for PII, SOC 2 Type II for vendor-of-vendor relationships). The online FS is in scope for: (a) PII retention and TTL enforcement, (b) data residency (the box must be deployable in-region), (c) at-rest and in-transit encryption (TLS gap on beava is the immediate blocker), (d) audit log of who-read-which-feature for sensitive decisions, (e) consistent point-in-time semantics for any feature that feeds a regulator-facing decision. Most managed competitors (Tecton, SageMaker FS, Vertex AI FS, Databricks Feature Serving) ship SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / HIPAA-eligible postures by default; beava in v0 cannot match without TLS, auth, and audit log.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A working online-FS demo (define @bv.event for transactions, define 30 features across 4 entity grains in @bv.table, point a notebook XGBoost scorer at the batch_get endpoint) can stand up in 1–3 days on beava given the existing fraud demo scaffolding in the repo. A production-ready rig with offline / online parity, materialisation from the warehouse, and a deployed scorer is typically a 2–6 week effort matching the published Tecton / Hopsworks 'first feature in 30 days' benchmark.

competition.incumbents: Generic / horizontal: Tecton (now Databricks, the visible market leader for managed real-time feature stores), Feast (Linux Foundation open-source default, online tier typically Redis or DynamoDB), Hopsworks (AI lakehouse with first-class feature store, RonDB / on-prem strength), Chalk (real-time ML / feature platform, fraud-focused), Fennel (ex-Facebook team, fully managed), Featureform (virtual feature store — plug into your own offline + online stores), Tacnode (newer entrant), Alibaba FeatHub (open source stream-batch unified). Cloud-managed: SageMaker Feature Store (online on DynamoDB, offline on S3+Parquet), Vertex AI Feature Store (Bigtable online, BigQuery offline; reported ~30 ms server-side latency), Databricks Feature Serving / Databricks Online Feature Stores (Lakebase-backed). Build-your-own KV layer: Redis (Redis Enterprise reported 3× faster, 14× cheaper than DynamoDB by Redis's own benchmark), Aerospike (PayPal, Barclays, LexisNexis public case studies), DynamoDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Within the fraud / risk slice specifically: Tecton has the most-cited public fraud case studies (Coinbase, Plaid Signal, plus a published 0.8 ms feature retrieval / 100 M txn/day / 40% false-positive reduction reference). Hopsworks publishes fraud-batch and fraud-online tutorials and a Feldera + Hopsworks real-time fraud reference. SageMaker Feature Store ships an official fraud-detection example notebook (sagemaker_featurestore_fraud_detection_python_sdk.ipynb) and an end-to-end aws-samples/amazon-fraud-detector-end-to-end repo. MLRun ships demo-fraud as a fraud-specific feature store demo. Vertex AI ships an online_feature_serving_and_fetching_bigquery_data_with_feature_store_bigtable example. Redis publishes feature-store-for-real-time-AI/ML benchmarks and case studies. Beava is competing against this entire layer for the 'open-source self-hosted real-time online FS with first-class aggregation primitives' niche.
competition.beava_differentiator: Five differentiators in this category specifically: (1) Single binary vs the (Kafka + Flink + Redis + Feast) or (Tecton managed) two-or-more-box norm — meaningful for risk / ML teams that do not have a streaming-platform team. (2) 50+ first-class aggregation primitives baked into the server vs Feast / Tecton expecting upstream Flink / Spark to compute aggregates (Feast in particular is a fetch-layer, not a compute-layer) — beava collapses materialisation and serving. (3) Sub-millisecond TCP batch_get is faster than Vertex AI Feature Store's reported ~30 ms server-side, on par with Tecton's published 0.8 ms, and matches Redis-class online stores. (4) Push-on-event ingestion (HTTP/JSON, framed TCP, msgpack) without a Kafka requirement — most online FS competitors assume Kafka or a managed CDC pipe; beava accepts the webhook-style and mobile-SDK-direct-push patterns that Feast / Tecton do not. (5) Apache-2.0 with no open-core split vs Tecton (proprietary now Databricks), Hopsworks (open-core), Chalk / Fennel (closed) — the buyer is not negotiating against an 'Enterprise Edition' upsell down the road.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that block production online-FS adoption in this category: (1) No TLS / no auth on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 — every managed competitor ships TLS + IAM out of the box; for an ML platform team this is a procurement non-starter. (2) No in-process sharding and no horizontal scale — Tecton, SageMaker FS, Vertex AI FS, Databricks Feature Serving all scale horizontally; beava is vertical-only in v0. (3) No multi-region replication — global authorisation paths require active-active or active-passive replicated online stores, which beava does not have. (4) No first-class offline / online parity story — beava is online-only, so the buyer must build the offline side themselves (Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks) and guarantee consistency with the online aggregations they have re-declared in @bv.table; competitors ship offline + online jointly with point-in-time correctness primitives. (5) No materialisation-from-warehouse — beava expects events to be pushed; Tecton / Feast / Hopsworks all accept 'compute this feature in Spark and write it to the online store nightly' as a first-class pattern. (6) No multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs — an ML platform team hosting multiple risk teams cannot isolate them today. (7) No SDK ergonomics for tabular ML idioms — Feast and Tecton ship `get_online_features(entity_rows=...)` calls that map directly to scikit-learn / XGBoost dataframes; beava's get / batch_get is lower-level. (8) No 'feature monitoring' / drift detection — Tecton and Hopsworks publish this as a core capability for fraud / risk classifiers where label drift is constant. (9) No on-demand feature transformations at request time (Tecton's 'On-Demand Feature Views', which Plaid Signal specifically calls out). (10) No managed service or hosted offering — the buyer must operate the box themselves.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream: the online FS is normally fed by (a) a streaming pipeline (Kafka / Kinesis / Pulsar + Flink / Spark Streaming / RisingWave / Materialize) computing aggregates and writing to the online store, (b) a batch materialisation job (Spark / DBT in Databricks / Snowflake Dynamic Tables / BigQuery scheduled queries) pushing offline-computed features into the online store nightly or hourly, (c) direct application writes from microservices (the 'push-from-event' pattern). Beava maps cleanly to (c) — its HTTP/TCP push is exactly that pattern — and to (a) via a thin Kafka consumer wrapper, but does not natively serve (b) as a target sink (no bulk-load API documented for ingesting a warehouse-computed feature set efficiently). Downstream: the scorer is XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost / TabNet / TabTransformer / Logistic Regression / a rules engine; integration is via batch_get and a thin Python wrapper. ONNX / Triton model-serving deployments routinely sit alongside the online FS.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both rules engine and ML scorer in parallel is the dominant pattern in fraud / risk; beava is the feature substrate under both. The scorer is typically XGBoost or LightGBM in 2026 production (still the SOTA for tabular fraud per the recent literature), with TabNet / TabTransformer / TabPFN in growing use and large players (Stripe, Coinbase) increasingly running transformer-based sequence models on top of the same tabular feature substrate.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users in the generic online-FS-for-fraud framing yet. Comparable named case studies on competitor platforms: Coinbase on Tecton (millisecond withdrawal scoring, sequence features framework); Plaid on Tecton (Plaid Signal, ACH ATO detection via On-Demand Feature Views); JPMorgan Chase reported at 9 ms p99 fraud screening on Inferentia3; Tecton's published 0.8 ms feature retrieval / 100 M txn/day / 40% false-positive reduction fraud reference; PayPal on Aerospike (200k → 1M TPS); Barclays on Aerospike; LexisNexis (130M daily txns, 120 ms → 30 ms); MLRun demo-fraud as an open-source reference; AWS aws-samples/amazon-fraud-detector-end-to-end. Vendor reference customers for Feast / Hopsworks / Chalk / Fennel are extensive but mostly private.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] No specific beava Discord / GitHub Discussion thread on the 'online feature store for fraud classifiers' framing identified in this research pass. Broader community signal is strong — Feast GitHub, Tecton blog series on fraud and feature freshness, the featurestore.org community site, dev.to commentary on training-serving skew, and active Reddit r/MachineLearning / r/MLOps discussion on Feast vs Tecton vs Hopsworks for fraud — all of which confirm an active buyer-side conversation that beava could plug into.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: Partial. `/python/beava/demos/fraud/` (schema.json, events.jsonl) and `/crates/beava-bench/configs/fraud-team.json` plus `/crates/beava-bench/src/workloads/fraud.rs` and `/crates/beava-bench/tests/fraud_team_validates_against_agg_op_descriptor.rs` exist and cover the raw-event ingestion + aggregation side of the fraud / risk use case. What is NOT yet shipped as an example is the explicit 'plug beava into an XGBoost / LightGBM scorer at decision time and serve N features in one batch_get' integration demo with a Python notebook — the framing closest to how Feast / Tecton / SageMaker FS show themselves.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High / active adversary. Fraud and risk are the canonical adversarial-pressure domains; feature drift, label drift, and concept drift are all aggressive. This category inherits all of the adversarial pressure of items 1a–1c (CNP fraud, instant payments fraud, APP scams) and adds the ML-specific failure modes of training-serving skew and silent feature corruption. The online FS becomes the point-of-blame when the scorer mispredicts and post-mortems trace it to stale or skewed features.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: Beava is the wrong tool for: (1) The offline half of the feature store — historical materialisation, training-set generation, point-in-time correct joins over months of history all belong in Snowflake / Databricks / BigQuery / Spark, not in beava. (2) Feature materialisation from a warehouse — beava is an event-driven aggregator, not a Spark-job-result sink; bulk loading a 100 M-row precomputed feature table into beava is not the supported pattern. (3) Cross-entity SQL-style joins required for some 'graph-shaped' fraud features (ring detection, money-mule chains) — beava is keyed by primary entity. (4) Multi-tenant feature platform hosting (a vendor running multiple customer tenants on one box) without namespace isolation and per-tenant auth. (5) Multi-region active-active deployments where the online store must be the source of truth across regions. (6) On-demand / request-time feature transformations (Tecton 'On-Demand Feature Views') that compute features from the request payload itself rather than from stored state — those belong in the SDK / scorer code, not in beava. (7) Feature monitoring, drift detection, and feature-quality alerting — adjacent capabilities competitors ship that beava does not.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be a credible online feature store for fraud / risk classifiers in this category: (1) TLS on all three listeners and mTLS option. (2) AuthN/AuthZ — API keys minimum, ideally JWT / OIDC and per-namespace RBAC. (3) Multi-tenancy with namespace isolation, per-tenant quotas, per-tenant auth — so an ML platform team can host multiple risk teams. (4) In-process sharding by entity key to break the single-binary memory ceiling, with a consistent-hash routing layer so a buyer with 1 B entities can scale horizontally. (5) Cross-region replication (active-passive with bounded staleness at minimum; active-active is harder). (6) An SDK shape that maps directly to tabular ML idioms — `get_online_features(entity_rows=DataFrame, feature_view=...)` returning a DataFrame, matching Feast / Tecton ergonomics. (7) A first-class 'materialisation from offline' ingestion path — a bulk loader that can pull from Iceberg / Delta / Parquet on S3 and hydrate the online store at startup or on a schedule, so the buyer's nightly Spark job can write to beava without per-row HTTP calls. (8) Point-in-time correctness primitives or a documented contract guaranteeing that a feature's value at time T computed online matches what an offline replay of the same events would produce — Feast / Tecton market this hard. (9) Feature monitoring hooks — at least per-feature counters, distribution sketches, and a webhook for 'feature value drifted beyond threshold'. (10) Approximate-aggregate primitives explicitly catalogued (HLL n_unique, CMS top-K, t-digest percentiles) — partly in the 50+ primitives claim but worth verifying against the explicit list. (11) Per-feature TTL and eviction so 90-day profile features and 1-minute velocity features can coexist cleanly. (12) Audit log of who-read-which-feature for SOC 2 / regulator evidence. (13) A managed / hosted offering (single-tenant per customer) so risk teams who do not operate infra can buy beava. (14) Bulk export / change-data-capture out of beava (to Kafka, S3, Postgres) so the online store can replicate values back to the offline tier for parity verification and for monitoring. (15) Time-travel / replay API — 'what was the feature value at timestamp T' — required for offline training-set generation against historical state.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Mixed. The pure online-FS framing (just serve features to a scorer) does NOT require triggers — the scorer pulls features and emits an action. But buyers in this category routinely also want 'when counter crosses threshold' triggers as an adjacent capability (rate-limit a BIN, freeze an account, page the on-call) because the same beava state that feeds the scorer also feeds the rules engine. Competitors like Chalk and Fennel ship trigger-style 'reactive' resolvers; beava does not. So triggers are not strictly required to fill the online-FS role, but they are required to win the whole-platform sale against Chalk and Fennel.
